name: Esther Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the carpentry end of a small building crew, setting door frames and checking the stairs before anyone closes the walls. I have a trade certificate and a good eye for a crooked line, though my knees complain after a day on ladders. My partner and I have grown children, but we still have less than a month of bills saved. Our contractor pays poorly for this work, and there are few other building jobs nearby; retirement is a thought, not a date we can afford to name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a faster purchase order does not square a door frame. I would still ask who checks the order before the timber turns up short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The little bit of AI on office forms would not threaten my carpentry directly. But a missed week of site work already puts us near trouble, and I cannot use a thin bank balance as a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking the site shifts and check timber quantities against my measurements before cutting. In the first year I would bring our late-payment record to the trades union branch and ask the crew to raise the pay schedule together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious even in this mild picture. The software is small; the gap between two wage packets is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is on that payment record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three delayed Friday payments this spring, marked against the hours we actually worked. I would take the dates, not a speech about machines, to the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does a missed week affect home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would postpone the car repair first, and my partner would take the bus to work. The car cannot stay broken for long if I need to reach a site.

say: **Office AI** may speed orders, but carpenters still have to measure and fit timber.
Our **late pay** needs attention even if AI changes little.
think: My **thin savings** make a lost site week hard to absorb.
A faster **order form** will not fix the low wages behind my retirement worry.
do: **Keep** working site shifts and check timber quantities before cutting.
**Take** delayed-pay records to the union branch with the crew.
feel: **Anxious** about weekly pay, although the AI change is small.
S0.quote: The software is small; the gap between two wage packets is not.
fieldNote: Her **trade skill** gives her standing on site but little financial room.
She sees **late payment** as a collective issue independent of the modest AI change.

steps.text: Keep carpentry shifts and check timber quantities against measurements
Bring delayed wage records to the trades union branch with crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the site office will change before the hands on the saws do. I want the crews told when a software schedule cuts the days allowed for a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and planning might move faster, and management could ask fewer of us to cover more rooms in the same week. If my hours shrink at our present wage, there is no spare month to bridge it and not much building work nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record each proposed change to the site timetable and compare it with safe fitting times. In the first year I would ask the union representative to take that record to the contractor, then apply only if a posted local carpentry vacancy pays enough for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing hours through a tidy schedule nobody on site tested. I have seen what happens when the staircase is marked finished before the handrail is fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your record show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day a frame is delivered, the time needed to fit and check it, and the deadline the office entered. A door that does not close is a better argument than saying I dislike computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a usable vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real opening within reach by car, with the wage and weekly hours written down. Moving to another low-paid promise would not cover our bills.

say: **Site schedules** should be checked against the real time needed for safe carpentry.
I would challenge **shorter deadlines** with the crew rather than refuse all software.
think: Faster **office planning** could squeeze my paid hours.
Few **local vacancies** and a thin buffer limit any escape route.
do: **Record** schedule changes against actual fitting and safety times.
**Take** the record to the contractor through the union representative.
**Apply** only for posted local carpentry work at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a schedule cutting paid hours.
S1.quote: A door that does not close is a better argument than saying I dislike computers.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** appears as distrust of untested deadlines, not ignorance of site evidence.
She would **change employers** only for a posted local vacancy with enough hours and pay.

steps.text: Record schedule changes and take evidence through union representative
Apply for posted local carpentry vacancy only if pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the planning desks could change by 2028, while capable site robots would follow around 2031. We should not sign away three years of carpentry wages because a contractor bought a clever machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order lists and drawings might be handled by AGI first, but my hands still fit stairs. A robot able to do that around 2031 could take the final earning years I need; with less than a month saved, I cannot simply leave work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union branch to demand paid safety training and a written rule that a qualified person checks robot work. If a real, funded place opens, I would take the course; in the first year after 2028 I would keep working and apply for a posted local inspection role only if its hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am frightened of losing the last useful years of my wage. I can still do the job, and that is precisely why being replaced would sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course a real option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named place, paid days off site, no fee taken from our savings, and a safety certificate the contractor recognises. A leaflet about future opportunities will not pay for a lost shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when the robot arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I need the wage, and I do not know what retirement would cost us. I would price it properly only after seeing a real offer and our household figures.

say: **AGI in 2028** may change plans before site robots arrive around 2031.
Crews need **paid safety training** and a human check on robot work.
think: A capable **site robot** could remove earnings I still need near retirement.
Less than **one month saved** rules out simply leaving the trade.
do: **Demand** funded, paid safety training through the union branch.
**Take** an actual funded course place if offered.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only at bill-covering hours and pay.
S2.quote: A leaflet about future opportunities will not pay for a lost shift.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 desk change** from possible hands-on replacement around 2031.
Her **training condition** requires an actual place, paid time, funding and recognised safety content.
She rules out **retirement now** because the household needs her wages.

steps.text: Demand paid robot safety training through trades union branch
Take funded contractor-recognised robot-safety course if an actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection role if hours and pay cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years gives us time to test machines before they reach a live building site. The robot date is roughly 2034, and the safety rules ought to be written by people who know what a loose prop does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a few more earning years than in the fast picture, yet I would still need them. I will not gamble our small reserve on training for a role that may never be advertised here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a proposal for trial inspections to our union safety group and ask the contractor for a funded place on a robot safety course with paid time. In the first year after 2031, I would take that course if it actually runs, then apply for a posted local inspection vacancy only if the wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but there is time to make somebody answer in writing. An extra three years matters if they contain pay and a course place rather than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The frame alignment and the temporary support before a machine moves timber. I would want a carpenter on site with the authority to stop the trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is announced but no place comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my carpentry shifts and bring the empty promise back to the union group. I cannot call an announcement a skill or a new job.

say: **Five years** allows trials and safety rules before capable site robots around 2034.
Carpenters should have **stop authority** during machine trials.
think: A longer **wage runway** helps, but I still need those earnings.
Our **small reserve** cannot fund an unadvertised career move.
do: **Propose** site robot trials with union safety representatives.
**Take** a funded course if a paid-time place runs.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work only with bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious**, though a longer timetable gives room to bargain.
S3.quote: I cannot call an announcement a skill or a new job.
fieldNote: She uses the **extra runway** to press for specific trials and paid training.
Her proposed **job move** depends on both a real local posting and enough pay.

steps.text: Propose union trial checks of frame alignment, supports and carpenter stop authority
Take funded robot safety course if paid-time place runs
Apply for posted local inspection vacancy if pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger carpenters a decade gives them time to learn new equipment without giving up the hand skills. For me, the question is whether the years until 2039 actually pay enough to retire on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2036 could change drawings and orders, but capable hands-on robots follow around 2039. I may have stopped site work by then, yet our savings are too thin for me to promise that today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my site work and ask my partner to review our income, savings and likely retirement costs each year. I would also ask the union to seek a paid transition course; if a place is funded and a posted local role offers bill-covering pay, I would train and apply during the first year after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the money, though less hurried by the machines. Ten years gives us a chance to build a real cushion if the work keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set an earlier retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No date until we know what we can live on and whether our site wages keep arriving. I cannot call retirement relief if the next food and utility bills cannot be met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the annual review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our actual weekly pay, savings, household bills and the cost of stopping work. I would ask my partner to check the figures with me because both incomes matter.

say: **2036 AGI** changes drawings before site robots arrive around 2039.
A decade helps only if **wages** continue long enough to support retirement.
think: I may leave site work before **2039**, but current savings cannot promise that.
Our **retirement costs** need real household figures, not a guessed age.
do: **Keep** carpentry shifts while reviewing household retirement costs annually.
**Seek** paid transition training through the union.
**Train** and apply only with a funded place and bill-covering posted local role.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings, with more time to plan.
S4.quote: I cannot call retirement relief if the next food and utility bills cannot be met.
fieldNote: She makes **retirement timing** depend on household income rather than a fixed age.
She seeks **funded training** but would attend only with an actual paid-time place and credible local work.

steps.text: Keep site carpentry shifts while reviewing retirement costs annually
Seek paid transition training through trades union
Take funded transition course if paid-time place and bill-covering local role exist
Apply for posted local role if pay covers household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because it gives the site only three years before capable robots arrive. I would need funded training on paid days, a real local opening at enough pay, and crew authority to stop unsafe work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The people measuring a stair should be heard before a deadline is put on paper. I want the trades union at that table with the contractor.

portrait: **Esther Evans**, 58, leads carpentry on building sites with a vocational trade certificate and a skilled eye for unsafe fitting.
She lives with her **partner**, has grown children, lower pay and less than one month of expenses saved.
Few **nearby jobs** and late wages make her anxious even when AI only trims office tasks.
She distrusts **untested machinery**, yet would take a funded, paid safety course tied to real bill-covering local work.
Her **retirement timing** depends on actual household income, and she wants the union involved in site safety rules.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens her needed late-career wages when capable site robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded course place** on paid days and a posted local role at bill-covering pay would make transition possible.
Union-backed **stop authority** during robot work would protect safety on site.
headlineQuote: The people measuring a stair should be heard before a deadline is put on paper.
